title: Lower, More Predictable Latency
summary: Tools that can cut the rare long delays for alarms, voice and video, to validate in a pilot.

opener.promise: Tools for lower and more predictable latency
opener.problem: Now and then an alarm waits behind a large download before reaching the nurses’ station.

beats.heading: The alarm stuck behind a download

caption.headline: The alarm stuck behind a download
caption.takeaway: Most alarm messages arrive at once; a few wait behind downloads, and those late ones matter.
caption.technical: 802.11be’s scope includes improved worst-case [[latency|latency]] and [[jitter|jitter]]{{be-latency-objective}}; [[tail-latency|tail latency]] is the slowest messages’ delay.

beats.body:
A bedside monitor raises an alarm. Its message is tiny, but it shares the channel with a workstation pulling a large image. Most of the time it gets through almost instantly; now and then it waits much longer.

Those rare late messages, the [[tail-latency|tail]], are what matter for alarms, voice and remote procedures. The scope of IEEE 802.11be includes at least one mode capable of improved worst-case [[latency|latency]] and [[jitter|jitter]] {{be-latency-objective}}: a design goal, not a promised delivery time.
beats.bottomLine: For alarms, voice and remote procedures, the rare slow message matters more than the typical one.
beats.sceneDescription: A road runs from a bedside monitor to the nurses’ station. Each alarm message is an ambulance; a large download is a line of grey trucks on the same single lane. Most ambulances drive straight through, but now and then one gets stuck behind a truck. Each arrival adds a block to an arrivals board behind the road: a tall green column on the left for messages that arrived quickly, and a trail of red blocks to the right for the few that arrived late, labelled the tail. The board is labelled illustrative.

callout.title: Why some alarms arrive late
points: Alarms share the channel with large downloads
Most arrive at once; a few wait behind a download
Those late alarms are the ones that matter{{be-latency-objective}}

questions.q: How much lower is Wi-Fi 7 latency?
questions.a: There is no single figure: worst-case delay depends on load, device mix and configuration. The standard requires at least one mode capable of improved worst-case latency and jitter{{be-latency-objective}}, with no fixed bound; measure it in a pilot with your own alarm and voice systems.

beats.heading: Tools that can clear the way

caption.headline: Tools that can clear the way
caption.takeaway: Another band and optional protected [[twt|TWT]] slots can keep downloads out of the alarm’s path{{rtwt-optional}}.
caption.technical: [[mlo|MLO]] offers another link to contend on{{mlo-tid-mapping}}; supporting devices clear restricted service periods{{rtwt-protect}}.

beats.body:
Wi-Fi 7 adds tools that address different reasons an alarm waits. **[[mlo|Multi-link operation]]** can send it on another band when one is busy {{mlo-bands}}. **[[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]]**, an optional form of [[twt|Target Wake Time]], reserves protected time, and devices that support it pause before it starts {{rtwt-protect}} {{rtwt-optional}}. **[[multi-ru|Multi-RU]]** gives the scheduler more flexibility to use spare parts of the channel {{multi-ru-be}}.

None of them knows a message is clinically urgent: that still depends on how traffic is classified and prioritised.
beats.bottomLine: Each tool addresses a different reason urgent messages wait, on devices and access points that support it.
beats.deepDive: MLO lets traffic use the link that gains channel access first, with TID-to-link mapping steering traffic classes {{mlo-tid-mapping}}; an [[emlsr|EMLSR]] device exchanges frames on one link at a time {{emlsr-what}}. Restricted TWT is optional {{rtwt-optional}}; its service periods require supporting stations to end transmissions before the period starts {{rtwt-protect}}. Multi-RU allows defined RU combinations per station {{multi-ru-be}}. Priority comes from QoS classification (WMM access categories), not from these mechanisms themselves.
beats.sceneDescription: Wi-Fi 7’s road has two lanes, standing for two bands. An ambulance can take the lane with no download ahead. At regular protected slots, trucks that support them pull over onto the shoulder, so ambulances pass more often. The new arrivals board fills mostly with green blocks on the left, with a shorter red tail.

questions.a: It depends on the cause. MLO helps when one band is congested{{mlo-tid-mapping}}, Restricted TWT when long transmissions block urgent traffic and the devices support it{{rtwt-protect}}, and Multi-RU when the channel has spare fragments{{multi-ru-be}}. Priority still comes from QoS settings.

callout.title: How Wi-Fi 7 clears the way
points: [[mlo|Multi-link]]: another band when one is busy{{mlo-bands}}
Optional [[restricted-twt|Restricted TWT]]: supporting devices pause in protected slots{{rtwt-protect}}
[[multi-ru|Multi-RU]]: more flexible use of spare channel room{{multi-ru-be}}

beats.heading: A shorter tail, to validate in a pilot

caption.headline: A shorter tail, to test in a pilot
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 7 aims to shorten the late tail{{latency-histogram-illustrative}}; measure worst-case delay before rollout.
caption.technical: Results depend on load, device mix, client support and configuration; there is no standard latency bound{{be-latency-objective}}.

beats.body:
Side by side, with the same alarms and downloads: the earlier generation leaves a trail of late messages; with Wi-Fi 7’s tools in use, the tail can be shorter. The boards show the shape Wi-Fi 7 aims for, not measured values or an expected result {{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.

Wireless is one link in the alarm chain, alongside middleware, servers and alarm-management systems. Include end-to-end worst-case delay in acceptance tests and keep alarm systems in their manufacturers’ validated configurations.
beats.bottomLine: Treat Wi-Fi 7’s latency tools as something to validate: include worst-case delay for alarm, voice and video in acceptance testing, not only average throughput.
beats.deepDive: Worst-case latency depends on deployment: channel load, device mix, client support for MLO and restricted TWT, and configuration of traffic classes. 802.11be requires at least one mode capable of improved worst-case latency and jitter {{be-latency-objective}} but sets no latency bound. No figures are shown here because results vary by environment; evaluate latency-sensitive applications in a pilot before rollout {{latency-histogram-illustrative}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Two roads, one above the other, with the same alarms and downloads. Above, the earlier generation: one lane, and its arrivals board has a long trail of red late arrivals. Below, Wi-Fi 7: two lanes and protected slots, and its board has a shorter tail, labelled potential improvement, deployment-dependent. Both boards are labelled illustrative.

callout.title: What to test
points: Worst-case delay for alarms, voice and video, not averages
Busy-hour tests with real downloads running
End-to-end alarm timing, in manufacturers’ validated configurations

questions.q: Can we rely on Wi-Fi 7 for clinical alarms?
questions.a: Not on Wi-Fi alone. Wi-Fi is one link in the alarm chain, and 802.11be sets no latency bound{{be-latency-objective}}. Alarm systems should follow their manufacturers’ validated configurations and your clinical engineering testing of the whole path.
Busy-hour P95 and P99 latency, jitter and loss for alarms and voice, roaming interruption, voice quality and end-to-end alarm timing, alongside throughput.
